Context: Designed and executed a localized, 7.5-hour observational research study mapping spatial utilization, social behaviors, and environmental dynamics within university communal infrastructure. Modeled data collection parameters to track human behavior patterns while controlling for external sociopolitical and structural anomalies.
Languages & Tools: Manual Field Ethnography, Comparative Categorical Modeling, and Du Bois-Inspired Data Portraiture Frameworks, Google Sheets (graphing)
Methodologies: Observational Research Design, Mitigation of Volunteer & Convenience Bias, Multitasking Categorization Architecture, and Psychological Color-Mapping.
Outcome & Impact: Constructed a multi-variable visual portrait demonstrating that communal atmosphere was driven by localized group interactions rather than standard temporal baselines. Navigated complex data-structurization challenges regarding human multitasking to map distinct environmental correlations—revealing an 84% positive mood rate among active occupants. Delivered spatial layout optimization recommendations to university administration to better align institutional square footage with real-world student utility.

title: Technical Projects
text:
Investigating the Social Consequences of YouTube Watch-Time Optimization

Context: Analyzed a large-scale YouTube dataset (1.5 GB; ~600,000 videos) to examine how watch-time optimization influences exposure to health and political content. Created a focused subset of 22,193 videos by filtering for 22 health and political keywords associated with topics particularly vulnerable to misinformation and polarization. Investigated whether engagement-driven recommendation patterns sacrifice viewpoint diversity and contribute to informational “rabbit holes.”
Languages & Tools: Python - pandas & numpy for high-volume data engineering, scikit-learn for feature scaling and K-Means clustering, bertopic for semantic modeling, and matplotlib & seaborn for visualizations
Methodologies: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Unsupervised Machine Learning (Clustering & Topic Modeling), and Information Theory (Shannon Entropy)
My Contribution & Impact: I built and executed a machine learning and text analytics framework:

Behavioral Clustering: Engineered data features combining log-transformed duration and engagement metrics (views, likes, comments) to run a K-Means algorithm (\(k=3\)). Identified three clear algorithmic archetypes: Low-Impact Snippet, Factual Rundown (dominating with 94% of total watch-time), and Rabbit Hole Perpetrator (averaging an immersive 25+ minute retention depth).
Topic Modeling & Polarization Analysis: Coded a text-cleaning pipeline to extract custom-filtered auto-generated transcripts. Deployed BERTopic contextual embeddings to categorize dense ideological themes within the Rabbit Hole Perpetrator cluster.
Quantifying Viewpoint Diversity: Applied the Shannon Information-Theory Entropy formula to compute a Topic Entropy score of 2.80 and an evenness index of 0.84 within the long-form deep-dive cluster. Empirically demonstrated that despite topic distribution, the broader ecosystem isolates users into highly concentrated narrative silos.

Finding the Best Schools for Your Money: A Data-Driven Analysis of College ROI

Context: Compiled and analyzed a comprehensive dataset combining institutional demographic and financial data with state economic contexts. Evaluated short- and long-term financial returns across 1,173 four-year U.S. universities and examined the impact of regional employment rate on college return on investment (ROI).
Languages & Tools: R — tidyverse (dplyr for data manipulation & ggplot2 for scatterplot regression visualization), knitr for LaTeX summary tables, and Quarto for reproducible reporting
Methodologies: Long-Term Financial Metric Modeling, Macro-Environmental Control Analysis, and Bivariate Ordinary Least Squares Regression
Outcome & Impact: Developed a multi-tier financial framework calculating 1-year baseline payback periods, 5-year and 10-year wage premiums, and 5-year cumulative returns on investment. Uncovered a stark contrast in the types of institutions at opposite ends of the financial returns gap. Affordable public institutions achieved the highest cumulative returns on investment, whereas expensive private liberal arts colleges in the bottom tier experienced negative early-career returns. Using regression analysis, I found that ROI is largely independent of the state employment rate and is much more likely to be impacted by institutional traits.

The only real limitation of this project is the dataset size (199 news articles). While perfect for a class assignment, ML models can overfit easily on small samples.
If you want to turn this into a truly high-tier portfolio piece, try downloading a larger public dataset (like the AG News Classification Dataset or a larger Kaggle news dataset with thousands of rows) and run your exact same code on it. If your SBERT pipeline still hits 90%+ accuracy on a massive dataset, you have an bulletproof case study!
Would you like help adapting your code to a larger dataset, or do you want to work on writing the portfolio markdown file for this next?
Here is a blueprint for how you can structure this unified case study for a personal website, GitHub repository, or portfolio.

📂 Portfolio Title Idea
Comparative Benchmark Study: Modern Transformers vs. Traditional Statistical NLP for Short-Form Text

📝 The Framework (How to Structure the Post)

Introduction & Executive Summary

Start with a high-level overview of what you did and the ultimate takeaway.

The Mission: Evaluate how traditional statistical NLP methods (TF-IDF) hold up against modern deep learning architectures (SBERT / Sentence Transformers) when processing short, low-context text data (news headlines).
The Data: 199 news articles containing titles and high-level topics.
The Big Takeaway: Across both supervised classification and unsupervised clustering, deep learning dense embeddings systematically crushed sparse keyword-matching, raising classification accuracy from 75% to 95%, and unsupervised cluster mapping accuracy from 45% to 94%.


Paradigm 1: Unsupervised Learning (Topic Discovery via K-Means)

Explain the clustering experiment to show how you handle unlabeled data.

The Approach: You used K-Means Clustering (\(K=4\)) to partition raw article titles without letting the models see the actual topics.
The Hurdle: Traditional TF-IDF struggled heavily because headlines are too short to share exact keyword matches, forcing K-Means to dump almost everything into a single massive cluster (yielding a low 45% mapped accuracy).
The Solution: SBERT captured the underlying semantic context, enabling clean cluster separations and achieving an outstanding 94% mapped accuracy.
Include your side-by-side performance metrics table here!


Paradigm 2: Supervised Learning (Predictive Modeling via Random Forests)

Transition into your predictive modeling phase to show how you handle labeled data.

The Approach: You built a machine learning pipeline featuring Stratified Train-Test Splitting, 5-Fold Cross-Validation, and Hyperparameter Tuning (GridSearch) to predict article topics using a Random Forest Classifier.
The Engineering Touch: Highlight your advanced feature selection strategy—combining Chi-Square filtering with Forward Sequential Feature Selection to aggressively isolate high-impact tokens from the high-dimensional TF-IDF space.
The Result: Even with rigorous feature engineering, TF-IDF topped out at a 75% F1-score because it couldn’t capture word relationships. SBERT effortlessly hit a 95% F1-score by natively leveraging contextual deep learning weights.


Key Engineering Insights & Conclusions

End with a strong, professional conclusion that highlights your conceptual maturity.

Sparsity vs. Density: Short-form text inherently breaks keyword-dependent models like TF-IDF due to severe data sparsity. Dense embeddings are mandatory for real-world semantic search or short-text routing.
Production Readiness: While SBERT delivers elite accuracy, it requires higher computational overhead. This study serves as a framework for weighing the exact accuracy-versus-compute tradeoffs required in production environments.

GitHub repository containing: 1. README.md 2. A folder named /notebooks containing your two cleanly commented CoLab notebooks.



Targeting the 0.1%: Mitigating Emergency Department Over-Utilization

Context: Collaborated in a 48-hour data hackathon to analyze a large-scale regional healthcare dataset representing millions of patient records. Our team targeted emergency department “super-utilizers,” identifying that the top 1000 patients (0.1% of the patient population) accounted for 10.5% of all emergency department visits.
Languages & Tools: R - data.table for memory-optimized loading, tidyverse (dplyr for data wrangling, tidyr for data reshaping, and ggplot2 for data visualization)
Methodologies: Data Preprocessing and Statistical Significance Testing (Two-Sample T-Test)
My Contribution & Impact: I engineered a data pipeline to classify patients into geographic regions (corridors) based on FIPS codes. I then coded two primary analytical components:

The ‘Medical Commute’ Analysis: Visualized the percentage of clinic visits occurring outside patients’ home regions and graphed the reliance on the emergency department by corridor. After comparing, I concluded that a lack of local clinic access correlates with emergency room dependency.
Statistical Significance Testing: Conducted a Two-Sample T-Test confirming a statistically significant difference (\(p = 0.0185\)) in emergency reliance scores between Central and Non-Central patient cohorts, providing our team with the empirical support to propose expanding targeted clinic infrastructure to vulnerable corridors.

title: Hannah Rozenbaum
text:
Welcome to my website!
Hi, I’m Hannah! I am a rising junior at UCLA studying Statistics & Data Science.
My professional interest lies in using data to solve complex social issues. Whether I am cleaning and analyzing messy real-world databases, deploying and auditing local AI models, or teaching foundational concepts to the next generation, I view data as a powerful tool for community impact and education.



About Me

Passions & Career Interests

Data Science for Social Good: Inspired by my coursework at UCLA, I believe statistical tools can solve complex human problems. Whether evaluating models for algorithmic fairness, informing evidence-based public policy, or building human-first systems, I aim to leverage machine learning and causal inference to create a measurable, positive impact on society.
Data Storytelling: Beyond predictive modeling, I believe data is a powerful narrative tool. While qualitative archives already capture human experience, applying quantitative modeling allows analysts to derive clear insights from a massive volume of sources. My recent independent project applies NLP to oral histories to illuminate complex testimonies and preserve individual voices.
Teaching & Mentorship: I am deeply passionate about education! I tutor SAT prep, precalculus, and chemistry, and worked as an instructor at Lavner STEM Camps teaching Python, robotics with engineering and coding, graphic design, and physics/chemistry labs.
The Data-Education Intersection: Building on my experience teaching, I am intrigued by how data science intersects with modern learning. I actively audit digital learning environments, from investigating how engagement-driven algorithms shape viewpoint diversity to analyzing how rapid AI adoption impacts the critical thinking skills of student developers.




️ Academic & Technical Focus
At UCLA, my path covers rigorous statistical and mathematical theory, advanced software training, socio-technical evaluation, and applied execution.



Hobbies & Life Outside Data Science

The Great Outdoors: I love staying active outside, whether hiking, skiing, paddleboarding, or playing tennis.
Urban Exploration: I spend a lot of my free time exploring Los Angeles, often walking a few miles to discover local foodie spots, historic hotels, and parks.
Unwinding: When I’m not adventuring outside, you can usually find me solving the daily NYT games, crafting, running my Depop shop, or curating Spotify playlists.
